name: Chapter 6: Haloalkanes and Haloarenes
description: Classification, naming, preparation, SN1 and SN2, stereochemistry, elimination, Grignard and Wurtz, haloarene reactions, polyhalogen compounds

cards.term: Haloalkane vs haloarene: hybridisation of the C bearing X?
cards.definition: Haloalkane: sp³ (alkyl). Haloarene: sp² (aryl).

cards.text: Useful halogen compounds: {{c1::chloramphenicol}} treats typhoid; {{c2::thyroxine}} (iodine hormone), deficiency causes goiter; {{c3::chloroquine}} treats malaria; {{c4::halothane}} is an anaesthetic.

cards.term: Fully fluorinated compounds are being considered as?
cards.definition: Blood substitutes in surgery

cards.term: Why do halogenated compounds persist in the environment?
cards.definition: Resist breakdown by soil bacteria
Mono-, di-, poly-halogen compounds
X on a carbon attached to 1, 2, 3 other carbons
X on an sp³ carbon next to a C=C (allylic carbon)
X on an sp³ carbon attached to an aromatic ring (1°, 2°, 3° possible)
X on an sp² carbon of a C=C
X directly bonded to an sp² carbon of an aromatic ring

cards.term: Classify halides by the carbon holding X
cards.definition: CH₂=CH–CH₂Cl: Allylic; C₆H₅CH₂Cl: Benzylic; CH₂=CHCl: Vinylic; C₆H₅Cl: Aryl; (CH₃)₃CCl: Alkyl, 3°

sp³ C–X: alkyl, allylic, benzylic. sp² C–X: vinylic, aryl.

cards.term: Common vs IUPAC naming of alkyl halides?
cards.definition: Common: alkyl group + halide (ethyl chloride). IUPAC: halo-substituted alkane (chloroethane).
gem: both X on the same carbon (alkylidene halides). vic: X on adjacent carbons (alkylene dihalides).

cards.term: Common and IUPAC names of CH₃CHCl₂ and ClCH₂CH₂Cl?
cards.definition: Ethylidene chloride = 1,1-dichloroethane; ethylene dichloride = 1,2-dichloroethane

cards.text: IUPAC names: sec-butyl chloride = {{c1::2-chlorobutane}}; neo-pentyl bromide = {{c2::1-bromo-2,2-dimethylpropane}}; tert-butyl bromide = {{c3::2-bromo-2-methylpropane}}.
IUPAC names: vinyl chloride = {{c1::chloroethene}}; allyl bromide = {{c2::3-bromopropene}}; benzyl chloride = {{c3::chlorophenylmethane}}; o-chlorotoluene = {{c4::1-chloro-2-methylbenzene}}.
IUPAC names: methylene chloride = {{c1::dichloromethane}}; chloroform = {{c2::trichloromethane}}; bromoform = {{c3::tribromomethane}}; carbon tetrachloride = {{c4::tetrachloromethane}}.

cards.definition: Table 6.1

cards.term: How many structural isomers of C₅H₁₁Br? (Example 6.1)
cards.definition: 8: 1-bromopentane (1°), 2-bromopentane (2°), 3-bromopentane (2°), 1-bromo-3-methylbutane (1°), 2-bromo-3-methylbutane (2°), 2-bromo-2-methylbutane (3°), 1-bromo-2-methylbutane (1°), 1-bromo-2,2-dimethylpropane (1°)

cards.term: Dihalo naming in benzene: common vs IUPAC?
cards.definition: Common: o-, m-, p-. IUPAC: 1,2-, 1,3-, 1,4- (e.g. m-dibromobenzene = 1,3-dibromobenzene)
C is δ+, X is δ− (X more electronegative)

cards.term: Trend of C–X bond length and bond enthalpy from F to I?
cards.definition: Length increases (139 → 214 pm); enthalpy decreases (452 → 234 kJ/mol)

cards.term: Trap: which CH₃X has the highest dipole moment?
cards.definition: CH₃Cl (1.860 D) > CH₃F (1.847) > CH₃Br > CH₃I: F is most electronegative but the C–F bond is very short

cards.term: Reagents to convert R–OH to R–X?
cards.definition: Conc. HX, PX₃ / PCl₅, SOCl₂

cards.term: Why is SOCl₂ preferred for alkyl chlorides?
cards.definition: By-products SO₂ and HCl are gases and escape, leaving pure R–Cl

cards.term: Catalyst for 1° and 2° alcohols with HCl? And 3° alcohols?
cards.definition: Anhydrous ZnCl₂ (conc. HCl + anhyd. ZnCl₂ = Lucas reagent). 3°: just shake with conc. HCl at room temperature.

cards.term: How are alkyl bromides and iodides made from alcohols?
cards.definition: Bromide: constant-boiling 48% HBr (or NaBr + H₂SO₄). Iodide: heat with NaI/KI in 95% H₃PO₄.

cards.term: Reactivity order of alcohols with a haloacid?
cards.definition: 3° > 2° > 1°

cards.term: How are PBr₃ and PI₃ used?
cards.definition: Generated in situ from red P + Br₂ / I₂

cards.term: Why isn’t H₂SO₄ used with KI to make alkyl iodides? (Intext 6.2)
cards.definition: H₂SO₄ oxidises HI to I₂; non-oxidising H₃PO₄ is used instead

cards.term: Why can’t aryl halides be made from phenols this way?
cards.definition: The C–O bond of phenol has partial double bond character and is hard to break

cards.term: Why is free-radical halogenation of alkanes a poor method?
cards.definition: Gives a complex mixture of isomeric mono- and polyhalides, hard to separate; low yield

cards.term: Monochloro isomers from free-radical chlorination of (CH₃)₂CHCH₂CH₃? (Example 6.3)
cards.definition: 4: (CH₃)₂CHCH₂CH₂Cl, (CH₃)₂CHCHClCH₃, (CH₃)₂CClCH₂CH₃, CH₃CH(CH₂Cl)CH₂CH₃
1: neopentane (CH₃)₄C. 3: n-pentane. 4: isopentane (2-methylbutane).

cards.term: HBr + propene: major product and rule?
cards.definition: 2-Bromopropane (Markovnikov); HI similarly gives CH₃CHICH₃ as major

cards.term: Br₂ in CCl₄ + alkene: product and use?
cards.definition: vic-Dibromide (colourless); discharge of red-brown colour is a test for C=C
R–Cl/R–Br + NaI in dry acetone → R–I + NaCl/NaBr

cards.term: Why does Finkelstein go to completion?
cards.definition: NaCl/NaBr precipitates in dry acetone (NaI is soluble), pulling equilibrium forward (Le Chatelier)
R–Cl/R–Br heated with a metallic fluoride (AgF, Hg₂F₂, CoF₂, SbF₃) → R–F
Finkelstein gives iodide (not F!); Swarts gives fluoride. "Swarts = Super-reactive F."

cards.term: Electrophilic halogenation of toluene: conditions and products?
cards.definition: X₂ with Fe / FeCl₃ in dark → o- and p-halotoluene

cards.term: Why are o- and p-isomers easy to separate?
cards.definition: Large difference in melting points

cards.term: Why does iodination need HNO₃ or HIO₄?
cards.definition: Iodination is reversible; the oxidant removes HI

cards.term: Why can’t fluoroarenes be made by direct fluorination?
cards.definition: Fluorine is too reactive
ArNH₂ + NaNO₂ + HX (273–278 K) → ArN₂⁺X⁻; then Cu₂Cl₂ / Cu₂Br₂ → ArCl / ArBr + N₂

cards.term: How is iodobenzene made from a diazonium salt?
cards.definition: Shake with KI (no cuprous halide needed)

cards.term: Colour and smell of alkyl halides?
cards.definition: Colourless when pure; bromides and iodides colour on exposure to light; many volatile ones smell sweet

cards.term: Which haloalkanes are gases at room temperature?
cards.definition: Methyl chloride, methyl bromide, ethyl chloride, some chlorofluoromethanes

cards.term: Why are b.p. of haloalkanes higher than hydrocarbons of similar mass?
cards.definition: Greater polarity and mass → stronger dipole–dipole and van der Waals forces

cards.term: Order of b.p. for the same alkyl group?
cards.definition: RI > RBr > RCl > RF (bigger halogen, stronger van der Waals)

cards.term: Effect of branching on b.p. of isomeric haloalkanes?
cards.definition: More branching → lower b.p. (2-bromo-2-methylpropane lowest of its isomers)

cards.term: Why does p-dichlorobenzene melt higher than o- and m-?
cards.definition: Its symmetry fits the crystal lattice better (b.p. nearly the same)

cards.term: Increasing b.p.: bromomethane, bromoform, chloromethane, dibromomethane? (Intext 6.6)
cards.definition: Chloromethane < bromomethane < dibromomethane < bromoform
Isopropyl chloride < 1-chloropropane < 1-chlorobutane

cards.term: Why are haloalkanes barely soluble in water?
cards.definition: Energy released by new haloalkane–water attractions is less than that needed to break water’s H-bonds

cards.term: Why do haloalkanes dissolve in organic solvents?
cards.definition: New attractions are of similar strength to those broken

cards.term: Which halo derivatives are denser than water? Trend?
cards.definition: Bromo, iodo and polychloro; density rises with more C, more X and heavier X
Nucleophilic substitution, elimination, reaction with metals
A nucleophile attacks the δ+ carbon and replaces X, which leaves as halide ion (leaving group)
OH⁻ → alcohol; R′O⁻ → ether; NH₃ → amine; CN⁻ → nitrile; AgCN → isonitrile; KNO₂ → alkyl nitrite; AgNO₂ → nitroalkane; R′COOAg → ester; LiAlH₄ → alkane

cards.term: What is an ambident nucleophile? Examples?
cards.definition: Has two nucleophilic centres: CN⁻ (C or N), NO₂⁻ (O or N)

cards.term: Why KCN gives nitriles but AgCN gives isocyanides? (Example 6.5)
cards.definition: KCN is ionic: free CN⁻ attacks via C (C–C more stable). AgCN is covalent: C is bonded to Ag, so N donates.
Second order: rate depends on both [CH₃Cl] and [OH⁻]; CH₃Cl + OH⁻ → CH₃OH + Cl⁻
One step, no intermediate: OH⁻ attacks from the back as C–Cl breaks; transition state has C bonded to five groups

cards.term: What happens to configuration in SN2, and the analogy?
cards.definition: Inversion, like an umbrella turned inside out in a strong wind

cards.term: Transition state of SN2: arrangement of the three C–H bonds?
cards.definition: All three in one plane; Nu and X partly bonded on opposite sides
Hughes and Ingold
Spatial arrangement of groups around a carbon; (A) and (B) are mirror-image configurations

cards.term: Relative SN2 rates of methyl, ethyl (1°), isopropyl (2°), tert-butyl (3°) halides?
cards.definition: 30 : 1 : 0.02 : ~0: bulky groups block back-side attack
CH₃X > 1° > 2° > 3° (steric hindrance)

cards.term: Intuition: why is SN2 so sensitive to bulk?
cards.definition: The nucleophile must reach the back of the carbon, like knocking on a door crowded by bodyguards; three methyl groups block it completely
Polar protic solvent (water, alcohol, acetic acid); first order in (CH₃)₃CBr only
Step I (slow, reversible): C–Br breaks → carbocation + Br⁻. Step II (fast): Nu⁻ attacks the carbocation.

cards.term: Where does the energy for C–Br cleavage in SN1 come from?
cards.definition: Solvation of the halide ion by the protic solvent
3° > 2° > 1° > CH₃X: stability of the carbocation

cards.term: SN1 vs SN2 reactivity orders together?
cards.definition: Opposite directions

cards.term: Why are allylic and benzylic halides very reactive in SN1?
cards.definition: Their carbocations are resonance-stabilised

cards.term: Order of R–X for the same alkyl group (both mechanisms)?
cards.definition: R–I > R–Br > R–Cl ≫ R–F (weakest C–X, best leaving group first)

cards.term: Which undergoes SN2 faster: cyclohexylmethyl chloride or chlorocyclohexane? 1-iodo vs 1-chloro? (Example 6.6)
cards.definition: The primary (CH₂Cl) one; the iodide (I⁻ better leaving group)
(CH₃)₃CBr > CH₃CH₂CHBrCH₃ > (CH₃)₂CHCH₂Br > CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂Br; SN2 is the reverse

cards.term: Why is (CH₃)₂CHCH₂Br faster than n-butyl bromide in SN1?
cards.definition: Greater +I effect of (CH₃)₂CH– stabilises the carbocation

cards.term: SN1 order: C₆H₅CH₂Br, C₆H₅CH(CH₃)Br, C₆H₅CH(C₆H₅)Br, C₆H₅C(CH₃)(C₆H₅)Br?
cards.definition: C₆H₅C(CH₃)(C₆H₅)Br > C₆H₅CH(C₆H₅)Br > C₆H₅CH(CH₃)Br > C₆H₅CH₂Br; SN2 reverse (phenyl bulkier than methyl)
CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂Br (1°)
(CH₃)₂CHCH₂CH₂Br: branching is farther from the reacting carbon

cards.term: SN1 vs SN2 at a glance
cards.definition: Steps: SN1: two (carbocation)  |  SN2: one; Kinetics: SN1: first order  |  SN2: second order; Best substrate: SN1: 3°, allylic, benzylic  |  SN2: CH₃, 1°; Solvent: SN1: polar protic; Stereochemistry: SN1: racemisation  |  SN2: inversion

cards.term: What is optical activity? d vs l?
cards.definition: Rotation of plane-polarised light (polarimeter). d (+): clockwise; l (−): anticlockwise.

cards.term: Who made the first polarising prism?
cards.definition: William Nicol (Nicol prism)
Mirror-image crystals whose solutions rotated light equally but oppositely: foundation of stereochemistry
Tetrahedral carbon; four different groups → non-superimposable mirror images
A carbon with four different groups
Chiral: non-superimposable on its mirror image (like hands), optically active. Achiral: superimposable.
Achiral: C-2 has two identical CH₃ groups; rotated mirror image superimposes
Chiral: four different groups (H, OH, CH₃, C₂H₅)
2-chlorobutane, 2,3-dihydroxypropanal, BrClCHI, 2-bromopropanoic acid

cards.term: What are enantiomers? How do they differ?
cards.definition: Non-superimposable mirror images; identical m.p., b.p., refractive index; differ only in direction of rotation of plane-polarised light

cards.term: Is the sign of rotation related to configuration?
cards.definition: No: (+)/(−) is not tied to the absolute configuration
Equal amounts of two enantiomers; zero rotation; written (±) or dl, e.g. (±)-butan-2-ol
Conversion of an enantiomer into a racemic mixture
Spatial arrangement at the stereocentre is preserved; happens if no bond to the stereocentre is broken

cards.term: (−)-2-Methylbutan-1-ol + HCl gives (+)-1-chloro-2-methylbutane. What does this show?
cards.definition: Retention of configuration though the sign of rotation changed

cards.term: Three outcomes when a bond to a stereocentre breaks?
cards.definition: Only A: retention; only B: inversion; 50:50: racemisation
(+)-Octan-2-ol with inverted configuration (OH enters opposite to Br)
The carbocation is sp², planar: Nu attacks from either face equally → (±) product, e.g. 2-bromobutane → (±)-butan-2-ol

cards.term: Intuition: why does a flat carbocation lose "handedness"?
cards.definition: A flat plate looks the same from above and below; the nucleophile can’t tell which face was the original, so both products form
Heat with alcoholic KOH: H from β-carbon and X from α-carbon are removed → alkene
α: carbon bearing X. β: the adjacent carbon.
The preferred alkene has more alkyl groups on the doubly bonded carbons
Pent-2-ene (81%) major, pent-1-ene (19%)
Nature of halide, strength and size of base/nucleophile, conditions. Bulky base → elimination.

cards.text: Typical routes: 1° halide → {{c1::SN2}}; 2° halide → {{c2::SN2 or elimination}}; 3° halide → {{c3::SN1 or elimination}}.

cards.term: Aqueous KOH vs alcoholic KOH with R–X?
cards.definition: Aqueous: substitution → alcohol (OH⁻ nucleophile). Alcoholic: elimination → alkene (RO⁻ acts as base).
RMgX (Victor Grignard, 1900): R–X + Mg in dry ether
C–Mg covalent but highly polar (C is δ−); Mg–X essentially ionic
RH + Mg(OH)X: any proton source (water, alcohol, amine) converts it to a hydrocarbon

cards.term: Why must Grignard reactions be moisture-free?
cards.definition: Even traces of water destroy RMgX (RMgX + H₂O → RH)
Took a maths degree first; Nobel 1912 shared with Paul Sabatier (Ni-catalysed hydrogenation)
2R–X + 2Na in dry ether → R–R + 2NaX (doubles the carbon count)

cards.term: Why are aryl halides far less reactive to nucleophilic substitution? (4 reasons)
cards.definition: (i) Resonance: partial C=Cl double bond. (ii) sp² carbon holds C–X tighter. (iii) Phenyl cation unstable (no SN1). (iv) Electron-rich Nu repelled by electron-rich ring.
Cl lone pair delocalises into the ring, giving C–Cl partial double bond character

cards.term: C–Cl bond length in haloalkane vs haloarene?
cards.definition: 177 pm vs 169 pm (sp² C more electronegative)
NaOH at 623 K and 300 atm, then H⁺

cards.term: Effect of –NO₂ at o-/p- on nucleophilic substitution of chlorobenzene?
cards.definition: Easier: 4-nitro at 443 K; 2,4-dinitro at 368 K
2,4,6-Trinitrophenol (picric acid)

cards.term: Why does –NO₂ activate only at o- and p-?
cards.definition: The carbanion’s negative charge lands on the carbon bearing –NO₂ only for o/p, where –NO₂ stabilises it; at meta it never does

cards.term: Intuition: more NO₂ groups, milder conditions?
cards.definition: Each NO₂ is an extra "sponge" for the negative charge: 623 K → 443 K → 368 K → warm water

cards.term: Halogen on benzene: activating or deactivating? Directing?
cards.definition: Slightly deactivating but o,p-directing
Resonance raises electron density at o and p positions
1,4-Dichlorobenzene (major) + 1,2-dichlorobenzene (minor)
1-Chloro-4-nitrobenzene (major) + 1-chloro-2-nitrobenzene (minor)
4-Chlorobenzenesulfonic acid (major) + 2- (minor)

cards.term: Chlorobenzene Friedel–Crafts with CH₃Cl and CH₃COCl (anhyd. AlCl₃)?
cards.definition: 1-Chloro-4-methylbenzene and 4-chloroacetophenone (major, para)

cards.term: Why is Cl deactivating yet o,p-directing? (Example 6.9)
cards.definition: –I effect (stronger) controls reactivity; +R effect controls orientation (stabilises o/p carbocation)
"Halogens are bad hosts but good guides": they slow the reaction (−I) yet point the electrophile to o/p (+R)
Alkyl halide + aryl halide + Na in dry ether → alkylarene
2 Aryl halide + 2Na in dry ether → diaryl (e.g. diphenyl)
R–X + NaI (dry acetone) → R–I: Finkelstein; R–X + AgF → R–F: Swarts; ArN₂⁺ + CuCl → ArCl: Sandmeyer; 2R–X + 2Na → R–R: Wurtz; R–X + ArX + 2Na → Ar–R: Wurtz–Fittig; 2ArX + 2Na → Ar–Ar: Fittig

cards.definition: Paint remover, aerosol propellant, process solvent for drugs, metal cleaning
Harms the central nervous system: impaired hearing/vision; dizziness, nausea, numbness; burns skin and cornea
Solvent for fats, alkaloids, iodine; mainly to make freon R-22; formerly an anaesthetic

cards.term: Why is chloroform stored in closed dark bottles, filled to the top?
cards.definition: Air + light oxidise it to poisonous phosgene (COCl₂): 2CHCl₃ + O₂ → 2COCl₂ + 2HCl

cards.term: Update: NCERT says chloroform was replaced by ether as anaesthetic. Today?
cards.definition: Ether is also obsolete; modern inhaled anaesthetics are halogenated ethers like sevoflurane, isoflurane (halothane has largely been phased out)
900 ppm: dizziness, fatigue, headache. Chronic: liver (metabolised to phosgene) and kidney damage

cards.term: Iodoform: former use and why antiseptic?
cards.definition: Antiseptic; action due to liberated iodine, not iodoform itself; replaced due to smell
Refrigerants, aerosol propellants, feedstock for CFCs, pharmaceuticals, solvent; formerly cleaning fluid, spot remover, fire extinguisher
Possible liver cancer, nerve damage, irregular heartbeat; depletes ozone
Chlorofluorocarbons of methane and ethane: stable, non-toxic, easily liquefiable. Freon 12 = CCl₂F₂, made by Swarts reaction from CCl₄.
They reach the stratosphere unchanged and start radical chain reactions that deplete ozone
p,p′-Dichlorodiphenyltrichloroethane; made 1873, insecticidal action found by Paul Müller (1939; Nobel 1948)
Insect resistance, toxic to fish, very stable and fat-soluble: accumulates in fatty tissue (biomagnification)
R–OH + SOCl₂: R–Cl + SO₂ + HCl; R–X + alc. KOH: Alkene (Saytzeff); R–X + aq. KOH: Alcohol; R–X + Mg (dry ether): RMgX; ArCl + NaOH, 623 K, 300 atm: Phenol; ArCl + Cl₂/FeCl₃: o- and p-dichlorobenzene
